blocks.text: There are three main types of half-cell whose E° value can be obtained when connected to a standard hydrogen electrode (SHE):

Figure 10.5 shows how to measure the E° value for a Cu²⁺/Cu half-cell. The Cu²⁺/Cu half-cell is connected to the SHE and the voltage measured. The voltage is +0.34 V. The copper is the positive terminal (positive pole) of the cell and the SHE is the negative terminal. The two half-equations are:

blocks.alt: A Cu2+/Cu half-cell joined to a standard hydrogen electrode. Left beaker: a copper rod marked Cu in Cu2+ (1 mol/dm3), terminal +. Right beaker: the hydrogen electrode with H2 (g) at 1 atm, H+ (1 mol/dm3) and platinum, terminal -. A salt bridge joins the solutions, the temperature is 298 K, and a voltmeter on the connecting wire reads 0.34 V; arrows on the wire run from the hydrogen electrode to the copper rod, with e- marked at both ends.
blocks.caption: Figure 10.5: Measuring the standard electrode potential of a Cu2+/Cu half-cell (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 10.5).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed Figure 10.5 draws the e⁻ arrows on the wire from the copper (+) electrode to the SHE (–). Electrons flow from the negative SHE to the positive copper electrode, as drawn above; Cu⁺² is written Cu²⁺.

The E° values show us that Cu²⁺ ions are easier to reduce than H⁺ ions (they have a more positive E° value). Cu²⁺ ions are more likely to gain electrons than H⁺ ions. So Cu²⁺ ions will accept electrons from the H⁺/H₂ half-cell and H₂ will lose electrons to the Cu²⁺/Cu half-cell.

Figure 10.6 shows how to measure the E° value for a Zn²⁺/Zn half-cell. The voltage of the Zn²⁺/Zn half-cell is –0.76 V. Zinc metal is the negative terminal (negative pole) of the cell and the hydrogen electrode is the positive terminal.

The E° values show us that Zn²⁺ ions are more difficult to reduce than H⁺ ions (they have a more negative E° value). Zn²⁺ ions are less likely to gain electrons than H⁺ ions. So, Zn will lose electrons to the H⁺/H₂ half-cell and H⁺ ions will gain electrons from the Zn²⁺/Zn half-cell.

blocks.alt: A Zn2+/Zn half-cell joined to a standard hydrogen electrode. Left beaker: a zinc rod marked Zn in Zn2+ (1 mol/dm3), terminal -. Right beaker: the hydrogen electrode with H2 (g) at 1 atm, H+ (1 mol/dm3) and platinum, terminal +. A salt bridge joins the solutions, the temperature is 298 K, and the voltmeter reads 0.76 V; e- is marked at both ends of the wire.
blocks.caption: Figure 10.6: Measuring the standard electrode potential of a Zn2+/Zn half-cell (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 10.6).

blocks.text: From these two examples, we can see that:

blocks.title: Quick Check 10.6
blocks.text:
a) Explain the following keeping in view the standard electrode potential values (E° Cl₂/2Cl⁻ = +1.36 V E°Br₂/2Br⁻ = +1.07 V, E° I₂/2I⁻ = +0.54 V)
i. The aqueous solution of iodine can be oxidized with bromine of iodide ions.
ii. Why bromine does not react with chloride ions.
b) Give answers using E° values (E°Ag⁺/Ag = + 0.80 V, E°Cr²⁺/Cr = - 0.91 V, E°Fe²⁺/Fe = - 0.44 V
i. Which of Ag⁺, Cr₂+ and Fe₂⁺, is the strongest oxidizing agent? Which is the least oxidizing?
Explain with reason.
ii. Arrange Ag, Cr and Fe in increasing order of their reducing powers.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Quick Check 10.6 b (i) prints the ions as Cr₂+ and Fe₂⁺; they are Cr²⁺ and Fe²⁺, the ions whose E° values are given.
